questions.q: Why does the "mass ↔ battery ↔ power" loop have to be solved by iteration?
options: A cell adds mass, and with it the power and the energy needed grow
Cell capacity drops with every charge cycle and must be recomputed
The motor table gives only five throttle points, so it needs interpolation
Python cannot solve nonlinear equations in closed form without a loop
questions.explain: Energy is needed for the power, the power grows as m^1.5, the mass grows with the battery: the quantities form a loop, and the solution is found by successive approximation.

questions.q: The ideal hover power from momentum theory is…
options: T² / (2·ρ·A)
questions.explain: P_ideal = T·v_i, v_i = √(T/(2ρA)), hence T^1.5/√(2ρA). The real power is 1/FM times larger.

questions.q: A motor with a 15×5 prop gives 1430 g at 173 W, and the ideal power for that thrust is 99 W. What does FM_sys ≈ 0.57 mean?
options: 57 % of the electrical power goes into ideal flow power
The prop runs at 57 % of its maximum RPM from the table
57 % of the thrust is lost to interaction between neighboring props
The ESC alone is 57 % efficient, the motor and prop are ideal
questions.explain: The system FM is referred to the electrical power from the table, so it includes the aerodynamic losses of the prop and the efficiency of the motor and ESC.

questions.q: A 4.29 kg vehicle: on four 15″ props the disc loading is 92 N/m², on four 17″ props 72 N/m². What happens to the hover power when moving to 17″?
options: It grows: a larger prop is harder to spin up
It does not change: the vehicle mass is the same
It drops by about 13 %
It halves: power ∝ disc area
questions.explain: The specific power P/T = √(DL/2ρ)/FM: lower disc loading means lower power. √(72/92) ≈ 0.88, corrected for a slightly different FM, gives about 13 %; in the example 464 → 403 W.

questions.q: A pack of P45B: 16.2 Wh and 70 g per cell, +10 % for the build, DoD 85 %, reserve 20 %. How much energy per kilogram of pack actually goes into the flight?
questions.explain: 231 Wh/kg per cell → ≈210 with the build → × 0.85 × 0.8 ≈ 143 Wh/kg. The other options are intermediate steps of the calculation.

questions.q: The 15″ quad gives 25.1 min against a 25 min requirement, but T/W on a sagged battery is 1.51. The right decision?
options: Accept: the time requirement is met, the rest is secondary
Reject: no thrust margin by the end of the discharge
Raise `MOT_THST_HOVER` to 0.66 by hand before the flight
Add one more parallel cell and recompute the time
questions.explain: T/W ≥ 2 is a separate requirement: by the end of the discharge it hovers at about 66 % of its maximum thrust and has nothing left to fight the wind. An extra cell means more mass and even lower T/W; a larger disc (17″) or more motors (a hexa) helps.

questions.q: The motor table was taken at 22.2 V, while Li-ion under load in the second half of the discharge gives about 20.4 V. How does the maximum thrust change?
options: It drops by about (20.4/22.2)² ≈ 0.84
It drops by 20.4/22.2 ≈ 0.92, linearly
It does not change: the ESC holds the set RPM
It grows thanks to the higher current at sag
questions.explain: RPM ∝ voltage, thrust ∝ RPM², so it is ∝ U². That is why T/W is checked on a sagged battery, not a charged one.

questions.q: The mission requires a 70-minute survey of a linear route, takeoff from a field without a runway, hover only at takeoff and landing. Which configuration?
options: An octocopter with a 6S8P battery on the largest frame
A quadcopter with coaxial X8 props
VTOL (QuadPlane)
A hexacopter on the largest-diameter props
questions.explain: A multirotor hits a ceiling at 30–40 min: the time grows as f_battery/√m. A wing spends P = W·V/(L/D)/η, several times less than hover; VTOL pays +20–30 % mass for takeoff without a runway.
